p.src: Now when Pang Tong heard these words, he was startled; he turned quickly to look at the speaker and saw that it was none other than Xu Shu. Seeing that it was an old friend, Pang Tong's heart was set at ease; he glanced around and, finding no one nearby, said, “If you expose my plan, it will be a pity for the people of the eighty-one prefectures south of the river, for you will have delivered them all to ruin!” Xu Shu laughed and said, “And what of the lives of the eight hundred and thirty thousand men here?” Pang Tong said, “Do you truly mean to thwart my plan, Yuanzhi?” Xu Shu replied, “I remain grateful for Imperial Uncle Liu's great kindness and have never forgotten my duty to repay it. Cao Cao drove my mother to her death, and I have already declared that I will devise no stratagem for him as long as I live. How, then, could I be willing to ruin your excellent plan? But I too am here with the army. Once it is defeated, jade and stone will be destroyed together; how could I escape disaster? You must show me a way to escape; then I shall seal my lips and keep far away.” Pang Tong laughed and said, “With such lofty insight and foresight as yours, Yuanzhi, surely this can present no difficulty!” Xu Shu said, “I beg you, sir, to instruct me.” Pang Tong leaned close to Xu Shu's ear and whispered a few words. Xu Shu was overjoyed and bowed in thanks. Pang Tong took leave of Xu Shu, disembarked, and returned alone to Jiangdong.

p.src: That very night, Xu Shu secretly sent trusted men among the various camps to spread a rumor. The next day, men throughout the camps gathered in groups of three and five, whispering among themselves. Before long, an informant reported to Cao Cao: “Word is spreading through the army that Han Sui and Ma Teng of Xiliang have rebelled and are fighting their way toward the capital, Xu.” Cao Cao was greatly alarmed. He hastily assembled his advisers and said, “When I led the army south, the only men who troubled me were Han Sui and Ma Teng. Though we do not yet know whether this army rumor is true or false, we cannot fail to guard against it.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, Xu Shu stepped forward and said, “I have had the honor of being accepted into the Prime Minister's service, yet regret that I have rendered not the slightest service in return. I ask for three thousand troops, that I may hasten through the night to San Pass and hold its strategic defile. Should any emergency arise, I shall send another report.” Cao Cao said delightedly, “If you go, Yuanzhi, I shall have nothing to fear. There are troops already stationed at San Pass; you shall command them as well. I shall now assign you three thousand infantrymen and appoint Zang Ba as your vanguard. Set out through the night without delay.” Xu Shu took leave of Cao Cao and departed at once with Zang Ba. This was the stratagem by which Pang Tong saved Xu Shu. A later poet wrote:

p.src: After sending Xu Shu away, Cao Cao felt somewhat reassured. He mounted his horse and first inspected the land camps along the river, then the naval camps. He boarded a great ship bearing at its center a banner inscribed “Commander.” Naval camps were arrayed on either side, and a thousand bows and crossbows lay concealed aboard. Cao Cao took his place upon it. It was the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, in the winter of the twelfth year of Jian'an. The sky was clear, the wind gentle, and the waves still. Cao Cao ordered, “Prepare wine and music aboard the great ship. Tonight I wish to feast with my generals.”

u.src: It was the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, in the winter of the twelfth year of Jian'an. The sky was clear, the wind gentle, and the waves still.
Cao Cao ordered, “Prepare wine and music aboard the great ship. Tonight I wish to feast with my generals.”

p.src: As evening drew on, the moon rose over the eastern hills, shining as brightly as day. The broad sweep of the Yangtze resembled a bolt of white silk stretched across the land. Cao Cao sat aboard the great ship, attended on either side by several hundred guards, all clad in brocade robes and embroidered jackets and bearing spears and halberds. The civil and military officers sat in their appointed order. Cao Cao saw the picturesque slopes of Mount Nanping, looked east toward the lands of Chaisang, west upon the waters of Xiakou, south to Mount Fan, and north to Wulin. Delighted by the vast prospect on every side, he said to his officers, “Since I first raised a righteous army, I have rid the state of villains and evildoers, vowing to pacify the four seas and subdue the whole realm. Only the lands south of the river have eluded me. Now I command a million valiant troops and can further rely upon the devoted service of you gentlemen. How could we fail to succeed? Once Jiangnan is subdued and all beneath Heaven is at peace, I shall share wealth and honor with you and together we shall enjoy the age of tranquility.” All the civil and military officers rose and offered thanks, saying, “May we soon return singing songs of victory. For the rest of our lives, we shall all depend upon the Prime Minister's favor and protection.” Cao Cao was delighted and ordered his attendants to serve the wine.

p.src: They drank until midnight. Deep in his cups, Cao Cao pointed toward the southern bank and said, “Zhou Yu and Lu Su do not understand Heaven's timing. Fortunately, there is now a defector who will become a mortal danger within their very midst. Heaven itself is aiding me.” Xun You said, “Prime Minister, speak no more of this, lest the secret leak out.” Cao Cao laughed loudly. “Every gentleman at this table and every attendant around me is my trusted confidant. What harm is there in speaking of it?” Then, pointing toward Xiakou, he said, “Liu Bei, Zhuge Liang—you fail to reckon your own ant-like strength, yet seek to shake Mount Tai. What fools you are!” Turning to his generals, he said, “This year I am fifty-four years old. If I gain Jiangnan, there is one particular pleasure I secretly desire. In former days, Lord Qiao and I were intimate friends, and I knew that both his daughters possessed beauty fit to topple a kingdom. Later, contrary to expectation, they became the wives of Sun Ce and Zhou Yu. I have lately built the Bronze Bird Terrace on the banks of the Zhang River. If I gain Jiangnan, I shall take the Two Qiaos as wives and lodge them upon the terrace to delight my declining years. Then all my wishes will be fulfilled.” With that, he burst into laughter. p.src: As Cao Cao laughed and talked, he suddenly heard crows calling as they flew away toward the south. Cao Cao asked, “Why are these crows crying in the night?” His attendants replied, “Seeing the bright moon, the crows mistake it for dawn; therefore they leave their trees and cry out.” Cao Cao laughed again. By then Cao Cao was drunk. Taking up his long spear, he stood upon the ship, poured a libation into the river, drained three full cups, then leveled the spear and said to his generals, “With this spear I broke the Yellow Turbans, captured Lü Bu, destroyed Yuan Shu, and subdued Yuan Shao. I penetrated deep beyond the northern frontier and marched as far as Liaodong. Ranging unhindered across the realm, I have hardly failed to fulfill the aspirations of a great man. p.src: When the song ended, the company joined in, and all laughed merrily together. Suddenly a man among those seated stepped forward and said, “When great armies stand opposed and the officers and soldiers must devote their lives to battle, why does the Prime Minister utter such inauspicious words?” Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Liu Fu, styled Yuanying, a native of Xiang in Pei, who served as Inspector of Yangzhou. Liu Fu had begun his career at Hefei, where he established the provincial administration, gathered the scattered refugees, founded schools, greatly expanded the tuntian farms, and promoted good government and education. He had served Cao Cao for many years and won much merit. Still holding his spear crosswise, Cao Cao asked, “What was inauspicious in my words?” Liu Fu replied, “‘Bright shines the moon, few are the stars; southward the magpies fly. Three times they circle round the tree, yet find no branch on which to rest.’ Those are inauspicious words.” Cao Cao flew into a rage. “How dare you spoil my pleasure!” With a single thrust of his spear, he stabbed Liu Fu to death. Everyone was horrified, and the banquet came to an end.

p.src: The next day, when Cao Cao had sobered, his remorse knew no bounds. Liu Fu's son, Liu Xi, petitioned for his father's body so that he might take it home for burial. Cao Cao wept and said, “Yesterday, in my drunkenness, I mistakenly slew your father. Regret comes too late. He shall be buried with the rich honors due to one of the Three Excellencies.” He also assigned soldiers to escort the coffin, which was sent home for burial that very day. The following day, Mao Jie and Yu Jin, commanders of the fleet, came before Cao Cao's tent and reported, “All the ships, great and small, have been duly joined and chained together. The banners and equipment of war are prepared in every detail. We await the Prime Minister's command to fix a day for the advance.”

p.src: Cao Cao took his seat aboard the great warship at the center of the fleet, summoned all his generals, and gave each his orders. Both the naval and land forces were divided under banners of five colors. In the fleet, Mao Jie and Yu Jin commanded the center under yellow banners; Zhang He the vanguard under red banners; Lü Qian the rear under black banners; Wen Ping the left wing under blue-green banners; and Lü Tong the right wing under white banners. Among the cavalry and infantry, Xu Huang commanded the vanguard under red banners; Li Dian the rear under black banners; Yue Jin the left wing under blue-green banners; and Xiahou Yuan the right wing under white banners. Xiahou Dun and Cao Hong were appointed to coordinate support by water and land; Xu Chu and Zhang Liao were appointed to patrol, guard, and oversee the fighting. The remaining valiant generals were each assigned to their respective units.

p.src: When the order had been given, three rolls of drums sounded from the naval camp, and the warships of each division sailed out through their respective gates. That day a sudden northwesterly wind arose. Every ship hoisted sail and drove through the waves and spray, yet remained as steady as on level ground. Aboard the ships, the northern soldiers displayed their valor with thrusting spears and flashing blades. Among all the divisions to the front, rear, left, and right, not a single banner was out of place. More than fifty small boats also moved back and forth, patrolling and enforcing discipline. Cao Cao stood upon the command platform watching the maneuvers. He was overjoyed, believing he had found a sure means to victory. He ordered the sails and awnings lowered for the moment, and the ships returned to camp in proper order. Back in his command tent, Cao Cao said to his advisers, “Had Heaven not favored me, how could I have obtained the Young Phoenix's marvelous plan? With the ships bound together by iron chains, we can indeed cross the river as though treading level ground.” Cheng Yu said, “The chained ships are certainly steady; but if the enemy attacks with fire, it will be difficult to evade them. We must guard against it.” Cao Cao laughed loudly. “Though Cheng Zhongde thinks far ahead, there are still things beyond his sight.” Xun You said, “Zhongde's words are entirely sound. Why does the Prime Minister laugh at him?”

p.src: Cao Cao replied, “Any fire attack must rely upon the wind. It is now the depths of winter, when there are only west and north winds. How could there be an east or south wind? I occupy the northwest, while all their troops are on the southern bank. If they use fire, they will burn their own army. What have I to fear? Had this been the season of the tenth-month spring, I would have taken precautions long ago.” They all prostrated themselves and said, “The Prime Minister's insight is beyond us all.” Cao Cao turned to his commanders and said, “The men of Qing, Xu, Yan, and Dai are unaccustomed to ships. Without this plan, how could they ever cross the perilous Great River?” Then two commanders stepped forward from the ranks and said, “Though we are men of You and Yan, we too can handle ships. We ask for twenty patrol boats. We shall sail straight to the northern mouth of the river, seize their standards and drums, and return, proving that the northern army can handle ships as well.”

p.src: Cao Cao looked and saw that they were Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, former officers under Yuan Shao. Cao Cao said, “You were both born and raised in the north. I fear you will have trouble aboard ship. The soldiers of the south travel constantly upon the water and are thoroughly trained. Do not lightly make a child's game of your lives.” Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan cried out, “If we fail to win, we willingly submit to military law.” Cao Cao said, “All the warships have already been chained together. Only the small boats remain. Each holds only twenty men. I fear they are ill-suited for battle.” Jiao Chu said, “What would be remarkable about using large ships? We beg you to grant us a little over twenty small boats. Zhang Nan and I will each lead half. This very day we shall sail straight to the southern naval camp and will not return without seizing a standard and slaying a commander.” Cao Cao said, “I shall give you twenty boats and assign five hundred picked soldiers, all armed with long spears and powerful crossbows. At daybreak tomorrow, I shall send the great ships of the main camp out upon the river to provide support from afar. I shall also order Wen Ping to lead thirty patrol boats to cover your return.” Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan withdrew delightedly. At the fourth watch the next morning, the men cooked their meal; by the fifth watch all preparations were complete, and drums and gongs could already be heard in the naval camp. All the ships left the camp and spread out across the water. All along the Great River, blue and red signal flags mingled together. Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan led twenty scout boats through the camp and sailed toward the southern bank.

p.src: Meanwhile, on the southern bank, the thunder of drums had been heard the day before. Cao Cao's naval exercises were visible in the distance, and scouts reported them to Zhou Yu. Zhou Yu climbed to a hilltop to observe, but Cao Cao's forces had already withdrawn. The next day, drums suddenly shook the heavens once more. The soldiers hurried up to a height and saw small boats charging through the waves, then swiftly reported to central command. Zhou Yu asked who among his officers dared go out first. Han Dang and Zhou Tai stepped forward together and said, “We shall serve as the vanguard and break the enemy.” Zhou Yu was pleased. He ordered every camp to strengthen its defenses and not to move rashly. Han Dang and Zhou Tai each led five scout boats out, one division to the left and the other to the right.

p.src: Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, relying on nothing but raw courage, came speeding onward in their small boats. Han Dang stood at the prow, a breastplate over his chest and a long spear in his hand. Jiao Chu's boat arrived first, and he immediately ordered his soldiers to loose a shower of arrows at Han Dang's vessel. Han Dang warded them off with his shield. Jiao Chu leveled his long spear and engaged Han Dang. With a single thrust, Han Dang stabbed Jiao Chu to death. Zhang Nan came charging up behind him with a great shout. From the flank, Zhou Tai's boat shot out. Zhang Nan stood at the prow with spear leveled as arrows flew thickly from both sides. Zhou Tai held a shield on one arm and gripped a sword in the other hand. When the two boats were seven or eight feet apart, Zhou Tai sprang across onto Zhang Nan's vessel. His blade rose and fell, cutting Zhang Nan into the water, and then he slaughtered the boatmen in all directions. The remaining boats turned and rowed frantically back. Han Dang and Zhou Tai urged their boats in pursuit, but halfway across the river they met Wen Ping's vessels coming toward them. The two sides drew up their boats and began to fight.

When the two boats were seven or eight feet apart, Zhou Tai sprang across onto Zhang Nan's vessel. His blade rose and fell, cutting Zhang Nan into the water, and then he slaughtered the boatmen in all directions.
The remaining boats turned and rowed frantically back.
Han Dang and Zhou Tai urged their boats in pursuit, but halfway across the river they met Wen Ping's vessels coming toward them.
The two sides drew up their boats and began to fight.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhou Yu led his commanders to the hilltop and looked toward the northern waters. Tower ships and warships filled the river in ordered ranks, their standards and signal pennants all properly arrayed. Turning his gaze back, he saw Wen Ping locked in battle with Han Dang and Zhou Tai. Han Dang and Zhou Tai attacked with all their strength. Unable to withstand them, Wen Ping turned his boats and fled. Han Dang and Zhou Tai hurried their boats after him. Fearing that the two might penetrate too deeply into enemy territory, Zhou Yu waved the white recall flag and ordered the gongs sounded. Only then did the two turn their oars and return.

p.src: From the hilltop, Zhou Yu watched until all the warships across the river had entered their naval camp. He turned to his commanders and said, “The northern warships are as dense as reeds, and Cao Cao is full of schemes. What plan can we use to defeat him?” Before anyone could answer, they suddenly saw the wind snap the central yellow standard in Cao Cao's camp and carry it into the river. Zhou Yu laughed loudly. “That is an ill omen!”

p.src: As they watched, a violent gale suddenly arose, and the river's billows beat against the banks. A gust swept past, whipping the corner of a flag across Zhou Yu's face. A thought suddenly struck Zhou Yu. With a great cry, he fell backward and spat fresh blood from his mouth. The commanders rushed to lift him, but he was already unconscious. Indeed:
